lessonTitle: Shear Flow and Shear Centre of Open Sections

blocks.text: A steel C-channel used as a floor joist carries a vertical load applied along its web, and under that load it twists as well as bends. Rolled channels in practice are often seen leaning over at the loaded end for exactly this reason: the load acted at the web, but the section's natural line of action lies outside the web, in empty space.

blocks.markdown: In an open thin-walled section, a vertical shear force $V$ is carried by **shear flow** $q$, the shear force per unit length of the wall ($q=\tau t$, in N/mm, where $t$ is the wall thickness). We assume linear-elastic behaviour, thin walls (dimensions measured along the **centreline**), a prismatic beam and a constant thickness $t$. The shear flow follows from the shear flow formula, where $I$ is the second moment of area about the neutral axis and $Q$ is the first moment about that axis of the area **beyond** the point of interest:

blocks.caption: Shear flow at a point in a thin-walled section; $Q=\int y\,dA$ for the portion of the wall between the free edge and the point

blocks.title: Shear centre
blocks.text: The shear centre is the point through which a transverse load must act so that the section bends without twisting. Equivalently, it is the point through which the resultant of the internal shear flow passes. For a section with an axis of symmetry it lies on that axis; for an open channel it lies on the horizontal symmetry axis but **outside the web**.

blocks.title: Shear flow distribution in a channel
blocks.prompt: A channel has a vertical web of height $h=150$ mm and two horizontal flanges of width $b=60$ mm (all dimensions on the centreline), constant thickness $t=6$ mm, with flanges extending from the web to the same side. It carries a vertical shear $V=20$ kN. Find the shear flow at the flange-web junction and at the neutral axis of the web.

steps.text: Second moment of area, treating the flanges as thin strips at $\pm h/2$ (their own $I$ neglected).
Flange: at a distance $s$ from the free tip, $Q=(st)(h/2)$, so the shear flow grows linearly from zero at the tip. At the junction $s=b$.
Web: $q$ rises parabolically from $q_j$ at the top to a maximum at the neutral axis, where $Q$ includes the whole flange plus half of the web.
Check: the shear flow in the web integrates to the applied shear $V$ (approximately, within the thin-walled idealisation).

blocks.answer: Flange tip: 0; junction: $q_j=94.1$ N/mm; web centre: $q_{max}=152.9$ N/mm (corresponding shear stress $25.5$ MPa).

rows: Flange, from free tip to junction
Web, from junction to neutral axis
Web, neutral axis to lower junction
blocks.caption: Shear flow in the channel of the worked example ($V=20$ kN)

blocks.markdown: **Locating the shear centre.** The shear flows in the two flanges give equal and opposite horizontal forces $F=\tfrac12q_jb$ at a lever arm $h$ apart, forming a couple $Fh$. The web carries the vertical force $V$. For the resultant of the shear flow to equal the applied load $V$ *and* to produce no net twist, the load must act at a horizontal distance $e$ from the web centreline such that $Ve=Fh$. For a channel this places the shear centre **outside the web, on the side opposite to the flanges**.

blocks.caption: Shear centre offset $e$ from the web centreline, away from the flanges (thin-walled channel, constant thickness). The thickness cancels.

blocks.title: Shear centre of the channel
blocks.prompt: For the channel above, find the flange force and the distance $e$ of the shear centre from the web centreline, and say where it lies relative to the web.

steps.text: Flange force from the triangular shear flow.
Moment equilibrium of the shear-flow resultant about the web centreline.

Direction: the flange forces are directed so that their couple is balanced by a load line on the side of the web away from the flanges; the shear centre lies 21.2 mm outside the web, on the opposite side from the flanges.

blocks.answer: $e=21.2$ mm from the web centreline, on the side opposite the flanges.

blocks.markdown: **Why loading through the shear centre prevents twisting.** The internal shear flow in the section has a resultant equal to $V$ acting along the line through the shear centre, and exerts no net torque about that point. If the external load acts through the shear centre, the external and internal force systems are equal in magnitude and have the same line of action, so there is no unbalanced torque and the section does not twist; it only bends. If the load acts at a distance $d$ from the shear centre, a torque $Vd$ must be resisted by torsion of the section. Open thin-walled sections are very flexible in torsion (torsion constant $J\propto\sum bt^3/3$), so even a small offset produces large twist and additional warping stresses.

blocks.title: Twisting moment from an offset load
blocks.prompt: A channel with its shear centre $e=21.2$ mm outside the web is loaded by a vertical force $V=20$ kN acting through the web centreline. Find the torque about the shear centre.

steps.text: The load line is offset from the shear centre by $e$.
Equivalent system: $V$ through the shear centre (pure bending, no twist) plus a torque.

blocks.answer: $T\approx424$ N m; the open section must resist this by torsion, producing a large twist angle.

items: Find the neutral axis and $I$ for the section.
Compute $Q$ at each wall point, then $q=VQ/I$ along the walls.
Integrate the shear flows in each wall to find the forces; use moment equilibrium for the position of the resultant (the shear centre).
Apply the load through the shear centre for pure bending; otherwise add the torque $Vd$.

blocks.title: Centroid is not the shear centre
blocks.text: For a channel, the centroid is on the flange side of the web, the shear centre on the other side. Loading through the centroid, or along the web, therefore produces twist.

blocks.title: Symmetry helps
blocks.text: If a section has two axes of symmetry (an I-beam), the shear centre coincides with the centroid. With one axis of symmetry the shear centre lies on that axis; for an angle or tee with thin legs it is at the junction of the legs.

points: Shear flow in a thin-walled section is $q=VQ/I$; in a channel it is linear in the flanges and parabolic in the web, with its maximum at the neutral axis.
The flange shear flows produce a couple $Fh$; moment equilibrium gives the shear centre offset $e=3b^2/(h+6b)$ from the web centreline for a constant-thickness channel.
The shear centre of a channel lies outside the web on the side opposite the flanges.
A load through the shear centre gives bending without twist; a load at distance $d$ adds a torque $Vd$ that the weak open section resists poorly.

questions.stem: A thin-walled channel section has a vertical web and two flanges extending to the right of the web. A vertical load is applied so that the section bends without twisting. Where does the load act?

options.text: Through a point on the horizontal axis of symmetry, outside the web, on the opposite side of the web from the flanges
Through the centroid, which lies inside the channel
Through a point on the horizontal axis of symmetry, outside the flange tips on the flange side

questions.correctOptionText: Through a point on the horizontal axis of symmetry, outside the web, on the opposite side of the web from the flanges

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the shear centre lies on the symmetry axis at $e=3b^2/(h+6b)$ from the web centreline, on the side away from the flanges.
distractorRationale.b: The centroid is on the flange side of the web, and loading through it produces twist.
distractorRationale.c: Loading along the web centreline leaves an offset $e$ from the shear centre and produces a torque $Ve$.
distractorRationale.d: The flange tip side is the wrong side: the flange force couple requires the load line to be on the side of the web away from the flanges.

questions.explanation: The couple of the flange forces must be balanced by moving the load line away from the web, away from the flanges. For the channel the offset is $e=3b^2/(h+6b)$, which for any real channel puts the shear centre outside the section.

questions.stem: At a point in the wall of a thin-walled section carrying a vertical shear $V=15$ kN, the first moment of the area beyond the point is $Q=9000$ mm$^3$ and the section's second moment of area is $I=1.8\times10^6$ mm$^4$. Calculate the shear flow $q=VQ/I$ in N/mm.
questions.explanation: $q=VQ/I=15000\times9000/(1.8\times10^6)=75.0$ N/mm. Dividing by the wall thickness would give the shear stress in MPa.

questions.stem: A channel has a web of height $h=160$ mm and flanges of width $b=70$ mm (centreline dimensions) with constant thickness $t=6$ mm. It carries $V=25$ kN. Find the shear flow in the web at the neutral axis in N/mm. (Treat the flanges as thin strips at $\pm h/2$; $Q_{max}=bth/2+t(h/2)^2/2$.)

A channel has a web of height $h=180$ mm and flanges of width $b=60$ mm (centreline dimensions), constant thickness $t=4$ mm. Find the distance of the shear centre from the web centreline in mm using $e=3b^2/(h+6b)$.
questions.explanation: $e=3b^2/(h+6b)=3(3600)/(180+360)=10800/540=20.0$ mm. The thickness cancels out of the result, so only the proportions of the section matter.

questions.stem: A channel has web height $h=140$ mm and constant thickness. If the flange width is doubled from $b=35$ mm to $b=70$ mm, by what factor does the shear-centre offset $e=3b^2/(h+6b)$ change?

distractorRationale.a: Would hold if $e\propto b$; in fact $e$ is quadratic in $b$ in the numerator, partly offset by the growing denominator.
distractorRationale.c: Would hold if the denominator did not change; it also increases.
distractorRationale.d: The geometry changes, so the offset changes.

questions.explanation: Doubling $b$ quadruples the numerator but raises the denominator from 350 to 560, so the net factor is $4\times350/560=2.5$. Wider flanges move the shear centre farther from the web.

questions.stem: Explain why a vertical load applied through the shear centre of an open channel section produces bending without twist, whereas the same load applied along the web centreline causes twisting. Describe what resists the twisting and why it is a concern for open sections.
markingGuide: The internal shear flow in the section has a resultant equal to $V$ passing through the shear centre.
If the external load has the same line of action, the two force systems are equal and opposite with no unbalanced torque, so the section only bends.
A load at an offset $d$ from the shear centre is equivalent to $V$ through the shear centre plus a torque $Vd$.
The torque is resisted by the torsional stiffness $GJ$ (and warping restraint) of the section.
Open thin-walled sections have small $J\propto\sum bt^3/3$, so the twist angle is large and warping stresses may be significant.
questions.explanation: A section twists only if the external loads exert a net torque about its shear centre. Choosing the load line through the shear centre removes that torque, and since open sections are weak in torsion, this is an important design aim.

questions.stem: A channel with web height 100 mm and flange width 40 mm (centreline dimensions, constant thickness 5 mm) has an 8 kN vertical load acting through the web centreline. Find the twisting moment about the shear centre in N m. (Shear-centre offset $e=3b^2/(h+6b)$.)
questions.explanation: The offset is $e=3(1600)/(100+240)=14.12$ mm, so $T=Ve=8000\times14.12=112941$ N mm $=112.9$ N m. Applying the load through the shear centre would remove this torque entirely.

questions.stem: Which statement about the shear flow distribution in a channel under vertical shear is correct?

options.text: It is uniform around the whole section
It is maximum at the flange tips and zero at the neutral axis
It varies linearly from zero at the flange tips to a value at the junction, then parabolically along the web, with the maximum at the neutral axis
It is zero in the flanges and parabolic in the web

questions.correctOptionText: It varies linearly from zero at the flange tips to a value at the junction, then parabolically along the web, with the maximum at the neutral axis

distractorRationale.a: A uniform shear flow would not satisfy the shear flow formula, which depends on $Q$.
distractorRationale.b: $Q$ is zero at the free edges of the flange tips, so $q=0$ there, and it is largest at the neutral axis.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: $Q$ grows linearly along a flange and quadratically along the web.
distractorRationale.d: The flanges carry significant horizontal shear flow; their resultant forms the couple that fixes the shear centre.

questions.explanation: The shear flow formula $q=VQ/I$ depends on $Q$, which is zero at a free edge and increases as more area lies beyond the point. In the flange $Q$ increases linearly with distance from the tip, and in the web it adds a quadratic term, reaching its maximum at the neutral axis.

questions.stem: For a channel with web height $h=90$ mm, flange width $b=45$ mm (centreline dimensions) and thickness $t=4$ mm carrying $V=10$ kN, derive the shear flow in the flange, find the force in each flange, and use moment equilibrium to locate the shear centre. State on which side of the web it lies.
markingGuide: Flange shear flow is linear from 0 at the tip; at the junction $q_j=V(bth/2)/I=83.3$ N/mm.
Flange force $F=\tfrac12q_jb=1875$ N in each flange, in opposite directions.
Moment equilibrium about the web centreline: $Ve=Fh$, so $e=1875(90)/10000=16.875$ mm.
The shear centre is outside the web, on the side opposite to the flanges.
questions.explanation: The couple formed by the two equal and opposite flange forces must be balanced by the offset of the vertical resultant from the web. Equating $Fh$ to $Ve$ determines the position of the shear centre.

questions.stem: True or false: for a channel section, a vertical load applied through the centroid of the section produces bending without twist.
questions.explanation: The centroid of a channel lies on the flange side of the web, whereas the shear centre lies outside the web on the opposite side. A load through the centroid therefore has an offset from the shear centre and produces a torque $Vd$.
